title: Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association (2015)
summary: An agency may change an interpretive rule without notice and comment because the APA exempts interpretive rules from that procedure whether they are new or revised.
notes:
Key line: "Because an agency is not required to use notice-and-comment procedures to issue an initial interpretive rule, it is also not required to use those procedures when it amends or repeals that interpretive rule." Justice Sotomayor, for the Court.

Citation: 575 U.S. 92 (2015).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were Thomas E. Perez, Secretary of Labor, and the Department of Labor, joined by three former mortgage-loan officers, Beverly Buck, Ryan Henry and Jerome Nickols, who intervened to defend the Department's position. Respondent was the Mortgage Bankers Association, a national trade association of real estate finance companies. The Department had issued the interpretation under challenge. The Association had asked for and then relied on the earlier, opposite interpretation and sued when the Department changed its view. The former loan officers had a direct stake because the new interpretation made them eligible for overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
sections.Material Facts: The Fair Labor Standards Act exempts employees working in a bona fide administrative capacity from minimum wage and overtime rules. The Department of Labor defined that exemption in regulations adopted through notice and comment in 2004, which listed employees in the financial services industry as generally exempt but said that an employee whose primary duty is selling financial products is not. In 1999 and 2001 the Wage and Hour Division said mortgage-loan officers were not exempt. In 2006, at the Association's request, it issued an opinion letter saying they were exempt. In 2010 it issued an Administrator's Interpretation withdrawing the 2006 letter and concluding that loan officers have a primary duty of making sales and are not exempt. None of these documents went through notice and comment.
sections.Procedural History: The Association sued in the District Court for the District of Columbia, arguing that the 2010 interpretation was arbitrary and capricious and that it was procedurally invalid under the D.C. Circuit's Paralyzed Veterans doctrine, which required notice and comment before an agency significantly revised a definitive interpretation of its own regulation. The District Court granted summary judgment to the Department in 2012, finding that the Association had not shown reliance on the 2006 letter. The D.C. Circuit reversed in 2013, holding that reliance was not an element of the doctrine and that the 2010 interpretation had to be vacated. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed on March 9, 2015.
sections.Issue: The APA requires notice and comment for legislative rules but exempts interpretive rules, and the D.C. Circuit had held for almost two decades that the exemption did not cover an interpretation that significantly departed from an earlier definitive one. The Department changed its view of whether mortgage-loan officers are exempt from overtime without any public procedure. Does the Administrative Procedure Act require an agency to use notice-and-comment procedures before it issues an interpretive rule that significantly departs from an earlier interpretation of the same regulation, or does the statutory exemption apply to revised interpretations just as it applies to initial ones?
sections.Holding: No. Section 553(b)(A) of the APA exempts interpretive rules from notice and comment without any exception for interpretations that revise prior interpretations. Because an agency need not use notice and comment to issue an initial interpretive rule, it need not use those procedures to amend or repeal one. The Paralyzed Veterans doctrine imposes a procedural requirement the APA does not contain and is invalid. The judgment of the D.C. Circuit was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Sotomayor began with the text. Section 553 lays out notice-and-comment rulemaking and then states that the requirement does not apply to interpretative rules. The APA defines rulemaking to include amending or repealing a rule, so the exemption for interpretive rules covers revisions as well as first interpretations. The D.C. Circuit had reasoned that a new interpretation effectively amends the underlying regulation, but the Court answered that an interpretive rule does not have the force of law and cannot amend a legislative rule; only the regulation itself carries legal force. The Court then invoked Vermont Yankee, which held that section 553 sets the maximum procedures courts may impose on agencies. Courts have no authority to add procedures of their own when the agency has followed the statute. The Court acknowledged the Association's concern that agencies could use interpretive rules to work substantive changes, but pointed to other safeguards: interpretive rules receive less deference and no binding weight, an unexplained change can be arbitrary and capricious under Fox Television, reliance interests must be weighed, and Congress can add procedural requirements in particular statutes, as it has done. Those checks, not a judge-made rule, are the remedy for abuse.

topics.lrs-n-interpretive-rules: Perez rejects a special notice-and-comment requirement merely for changing a prior interpretive rule.
topics.lrs-i-regulatory-deference: The concurrences by Scalia and Thomas questioned Auer deference and set up the later reconsideration in Kisor.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was unanimous, 9 to 0. Justice Alito joined the opinion except Part III-B and wrote separately to say the Paralyzed Veterans doctrine was an understandable response to the problems created by Auer deference, which he would reconsider. Justice Scalia concurred in the judgment and urged the Court to abandon Auer deference, since deferring to agency interpretations of their own rules lets agencies bind the public without notice and comment. Justice Thomas concurred in the judgment and argued that Auer deference raises serious constitutional questions about the separation of powers.
